# Unit 3: Monophasic liquids, suspensions and emulsions

Liquid preparations are the most common dosage forms prepared in a dispensing laboratory. Monophasic liquids are true solutions with one phase. Biphasic liquids have two phases: a solid dispersed in a liquid (suspension) or a liquid dispersed in another liquid (emulsion). Long questions on flocculated versus deflocculated suspensions, emulsifying agents, identification of emulsion type and stability problems appear very often.

## 3.1 Monophasic liquids

Monophasic liquids may be for **internal use** (syrups, elixirs, linctuses, drops), for use in **body cavities** (gargles, mouthwashes, throat paints, ear drops, nasal drops, enemas) or for **external use** (liniments, lotions).

### Gargles

- **Definition:** aqueous solutions used to treat or soothe the throat and pharynx. The liquid is held in the throat, agitated with air, and **spat out, not swallowed**.
- Usually dispensed as concentrated solutions, diluted with warm water before use.
- Contain antiseptics, astringents or mild analgesics.
- Examples: phenol gargle, potassium chlorate and phenol gargle, iodine gargle, povidone-iodine gargle.
- **Preparation:** dissolve the ingredients in purified water, filter if needed, label "Not to be swallowed" and give dilution directions.

### Mouthwashes

- **Definition:** aqueous solutions used to **clean, deodorise and freshen the mouth**, and for antiseptic or anti-plaque action. Used with or without dilution, swished in the mouth and spat out.
- Examples: **compound sodium chloride mouthwash** (sodium chloride, sodium bicarbonate, peppermint), **chlorhexidine gluconate mouthwash 0.2% w/v** (anti-plaque), hydrogen peroxide mouthwash.
- Ingredients: antiseptic, astringent, flavour, colour, sometimes a little alcohol.

### Throat paints

- **Definition:** **viscous** liquid preparations applied to the mouth or throat with a brush or swab.
- **Glycerin** is the usual base: it is viscous so it clings to the mucosa, it is sweet, and it has a mild antiseptic action.
- Example: **Compound iodine paint (Mandl's paint)** — iodine dissolved in potassium iodide solution, with peppermint oil and glycerin. Potassium iodide forms the soluble triiodide complex (I2 + I− ⇌ I3−).
- Others: borax glycerin, tannic acid glycerin.

### Ear drops

- **Definition:** solutions, suspensions or emulsions of drugs instilled into the ear with a dropper.
- **Uses:** to clean the ear, **soften and remove wax** (sodium bicarbonate ear drops, olive oil, hydrogen peroxide), and to treat infection or inflammation (antibiotic and corticosteroid drops).
- **Vehicles:** water, glycerin, propylene glycol, alcohol. Glycerin and propylene glycol are viscous and hygroscopic, so they stay in the ear and absorb moisture.
- Warm the bottle in the hand before use; do not use if the eardrum is perforated unless prescribed.

### Nasal drops

- **Definition:** solutions (or suspensions) instilled into the nostrils for local action (decongestant, antiseptic) or systemic effect.
- Should be **aqueous, nearly isotonic** and of pH close to that of nasal secretions, so that the cilia are not damaged.
- **Oily nasal drops are avoided**, because oil can be inhaled into the lungs and cause lipoid pneumonia; oil also slows ciliary movement.
- Examples: ephedrine nasal drops, xylometazoline nasal drops, saline nasal drops.

### Enemas

- **Definition:** aqueous or oily liquids introduced into the **rectum** for evacuation, local action, diagnosis or systemic effect.
- **Evacuant enemas** (cleansing, larger volume, expelled): soap enema, glycerin enema, phosphate enema, liquid paraffin (oily) enema.
- **Retention enemas** (small volume, kept in the rectum for local or systemic action): prednisolone and mesalazine enemas for ulcerative colitis; contrast enemas for X-ray.
- Warm to body temperature before use. Packed in disposable plastic packs with a nozzle.

### Syrups

- **Definition:** concentrated, viscous aqueous solutions of sugar (sucrose), with or without medicinal and flavouring agents.
- **Simple Syrup IP** contains **66.7% w/w sucrose** in purified water. At this concentration it is nearly saturated and resists microbial growth because the high osmotic pressure draws water out of microbes.
- **Types:** simple syrup (no drug), flavoured syrups (orange syrup, vehicle), medicated syrups (for example compound syrup of ferrous phosphate, paracetamol syrup), sugar-free syrups (sorbitol, saccharin, aspartame; for diabetics and dental care).

**Methods of preparation**

| Method | When used |
| --- | --- |
| Solution with heat | Quick; for heat-stable ingredients. Heat only enough to dissolve sugar |
| Agitation without heat | Heat-sensitive or volatile ingredients; slow |
| Percolation | Water passed through a column of sucrose |
| Addition of a medicated liquid to syrup | Tinctures, extracts or drug solutions mixed into syrup |

**Problems with syrups**

- **Inversion:** prolonged heating, especially in acid, hydrolyses sucrose into glucose and fructose (invert sugar), which is more prone to fermentation and darkening (caramelisation).
- **Crystallisation:** sugar crystallises at the neck of the bottle (cap locking) if the syrup is supersaturated or evaporates.
- **Fermentation and mould** in dilute syrups: add preservative or keep the concentration high.

### Elixirs

- **Definition:** **clear, sweetened, flavoured, hydroalcoholic** liquids for oral use. Less sweet and less viscous than syrups.
- Alcohol keeps both water-soluble and alcohol-soluble ingredients in solution and acts as a preservative.
- **Types:** non-medicated (aromatic elixir, used as a vehicle) and medicated (paracetamol paediatric elixir, piperazine citrate elixir).
- Other ingredients: glycerin, propylene glycol, sorbitol, syrup, flavour, colour.
- **Preparation:** dissolve water-soluble ingredients in water and alcohol-soluble ones in alcohol; add the aqueous part to the alcoholic part slowly with stirring (to avoid cloudiness), make up to volume, filter (with talc if needed) and pack in tight amber bottles.

### Linctuses

Viscous, sweet liquids used for **cough**, sipped slowly and swallowed without water so they coat the throat. They usually contain a demulcent, expectorant or cough suppressant in syrup base (example: simple linctus, codeine linctus, terpin hydrate linctus).

### Liniments

- **Definition:** liquid or semi-liquid preparations for application to **intact skin with friction (rubbing)**.
- **Vehicles:** alcoholic (aid penetration, counter-irritant and rubefacient effect) or oily (milder, lubricant, good for massage).
- Contain counter-irritants, rubefacients or analgesics: turpentine oil, methyl salicylate, camphor.
- **Never apply to broken skin** (pain and toxic absorption). Label "For external use only".
- Examples: **turpentine liniment** (an emulsion made with soft soap), methyl salicylate liniment, camphor liniment.

### Lotions

- **Definition:** liquid preparations applied to the skin **without friction**, by dabbing with cotton or a soft cloth.
- Uses: cooling, soothing, protective, antiseptic, astringent or antipruritic.
- May be solutions or suspensions. Alcohol in a lotion gives a cooling effect by evaporation; glycerin keeps the skin moist.
- Example: **calamine lotion** (soothing for itching and sunburn), salicylic acid lotion.
- Label "Shake well" (suspensions) and "For external use only".

| Feature | Liniment | Lotion |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Applied | With friction (rubbing) | Without friction (dabbing) |
| Purpose | Rubefacient, counter-irritant, analgesic | Cooling, soothing, protective |
| On broken skin | Never | Some can be used |

## 3.2 Suspensions

**Suspension:** a biphasic liquid in which **fine insoluble solid particles** (dispersed phase, usually 0.5–5 µm for oral use) are distributed in a liquid (continuous phase), usually with a suspending agent.

| Advantages | Disadvantages |
| --- | --- |
| Give insoluble drugs in liquid form | Physically unstable: particles settle |
| Mask bitter taste (insoluble drug is not tasted) | Caking may make redispersion impossible |
| Drug more stable than in solution (less hydrolysis) | Dose uniformity depends on shaking |
| Can give sustained release (depot injections) | Bulky; must be handled carefully |
| Suitable for patients who cannot swallow tablets | Need a preservative and good formulation skill |

### Classification

- **By route:** oral (antacid suspensions, paracetamol suspension), topical (calamine lotion), parenteral (procaine penicillin, depot steroids), ophthalmic, otic, rectal.
- **By particle size:** colloidal (below 1 µm), coarse (above 1 µm), nanosuspensions.
- **By the state of the particles:** **flocculated** and **deflocculated**.
- **By nature of the solid:** **diffusible** solids (light kaolin, light magnesium carbonate, magnesium trisilicate, bismuth carbonate), which stay dispersed long enough after shaking to give a dose; **indiffusible** solids (calamine, zinc oxide, sulphur, hydrocortisone), which settle quickly and need a suspending agent.

### Properties of a good suspension

- Particles settle slowly and redisperse easily on gentle shaking.
- No cake forms; uniform dose is withdrawn after shaking.
- Pours easily from the bottle (not too viscous).
- Fine, uniform particles; pleasant appearance, taste and smell.
- Physically, chemically and microbially stable.

### Stokes' law

The rate of settling of a spherical particle:

**v = d² (ρs − ρo) g ÷ 18 η**

v = settling velocity, d = particle diameter, ρs and ρo = density of solid and liquid, g = gravity, η = viscosity of the medium.

So settling is slowed by **smaller particles**, **smaller density difference** and **higher viscosity**. Because d is squared, halving the particle size cuts the settling rate to one quarter.

### Preparation of suspensions

**1. Dispersion method (most common in dispensing)**

1. Reduce the solid to a fine powder.
2. **Wet** the hydrophobic powder with a wetting agent (glycerin, alcohol, a surfactant such as polysorbate) to drive off air.
3. Triturate with the **suspending agent** (tragacanth, acacia, methylcellulose, sodium CMC, bentonite) and a little vehicle to form a smooth paste.
4. Add the rest of the vehicle in portions with stirring; add preservative, flavour and colour.
5. Make up to volume and pack in a wide-mouthed bottle with space for shaking.

**2. Precipitation (condensation) method**

- **Organic solvent precipitation:** the drug dissolved in an organic solvent is poured into water (for example precipitating a water-insoluble substance from an alcoholic solution).
- **pH change:** the drug is soluble at one pH and precipitates at another.
- **Double decomposition:** two soluble reactants form an insoluble product, for example magnesium hydroxide mixture (MgSO4 + 2NaOH → Mg(OH)2 + Na2SO4) and aluminium hydroxide gel.

### Flocculated and deflocculated suspensions

Particles carry a surface charge (zeta potential). If repulsion is strong, they stay separate (**deflocculated**). If repulsion is reduced, they form loose clusters called **flocs** (**flocculated**).

| Property | Flocculated | Deflocculated |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Particles | Loose aggregates (flocs) | Separate individual particles |
| Rate of sedimentation | Fast | Slow |
| Sediment | Loose, high volume, easily redispersed | Compact, small volume, hard **cake** that is difficult to redisperse |
| Supernatant | Clear quickly | Stays cloudy for a long time |
| Appearance | Less elegant (clear layer forms quickly) | Pleasing, uniform for a long time |
| Zeta potential | Low | High |

```text
   Deflocculated                     Flocculated
   (after storage)                   (after storage)
   |  cloudy liquid  |               |  clear liquid   |
   |  cloudy liquid  |               |                 |
   |  cloudy liquid  |               |.:.:.:.:.:.:.:.:.|
   |#################|  <- hard cake |.:.:.:.:.:.:.:.:.| <- loose floc bed
```

**Controlled flocculation** gives the best of both: flocs that settle into a loose, easily redispersed sediment, combined with a suspending agent (structured vehicle) to slow settling. Flocculating agents:

- **Electrolytes** (for example potassium dihydrogen phosphate, aluminium chloride) lower the zeta potential and form bridges.
- **Surfactants** (ionic or non-ionic) adsorb and neutralise charge.
- **Polymers** (hydrophilic colloids) form bridges between particles.

**Measuring suspension quality**

- **Sedimentation volume, F = Vu ÷ Vo**, where Vu = ultimate volume of sediment and Vo = original volume of suspension. F nearer 1 is better. Example: 50 ml suspension gives a 30 ml sediment → F = 30 ÷ 50 = 0.6.
- **Degree of flocculation, β = F ÷ F∞**, where F∞ is the sedimentation volume of the deflocculated suspension. Example: F = 0.6 and F∞ = 0.15 → β = 4.
- Ease of redispersion, particle size, zeta potential, viscosity (rheology).

### Stability problems and how to overcome them

| Problem | Cause | Remedy |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Rapid sedimentation | Large particles, low viscosity, high density difference | Reduce particle size, add suspending agent, adjust density (sorbitol, glycerin) |
| **Caking** | Deflocculated particles pack tightly | Controlled flocculation, structured vehicle |
| **Crystal growth (Ostwald ripening)** | Small particles dissolve and redeposit on large ones, especially with temperature changes | Narrow particle size range, protective colloids, steady storage temperature |
| Polymorphic change | Metastable form converts to stable form | Use the stable form |
| Microbial growth | Suspending agents of natural origin support microbes | Preservatives such as parabens |
| Chemical breakdown | Hydrolysis, oxidation | Buffers, antioxidants, correct pH |

## 3.3 Emulsions

**Emulsion:** a biphasic system of two immiscible liquids in which one liquid (**dispersed / internal phase**) is distributed as fine globules in the other (**continuous / external phase**), stabilised by an **emulsifying agent**.

### Classification

| Type | Description | Examples |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Oil-in-water (O/W)** | Oil globules in water | Liquid paraffin emulsion, castor oil emulsion, vanishing creams; most oral emulsions |
| **Water-in-oil (W/O)** | Water droplets in oil | Cold creams, oily calamine lotion, butter |
| **Multiple emulsions** | W/O/W or O/W/O | Used for prolonged release, taste masking |
| **Microemulsions** | Transparent, thermodynamically stable, globules below about 100 nm | Used for poorly soluble drugs |

**By use:** oral (O/W, oil taste masked), external (O/W washable, W/O emollient), parenteral (intravenous fat emulsions are O/W).

### Emulsifying agents

They lower interfacial tension and form a protective film round the globules.

| Group | Examples | Type formed |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Natural** (hydrophilic colloids) | Acacia, tragacanth, gelatin, egg yolk, pectin, methylcellulose | O/W |
| **Natural** (sterol-containing) | Wool fat, wool alcohols, cholesterol, beeswax | W/O |
| **Synthetic surfactants: anionic** | Sodium lauryl sulphate; monovalent soaps (sodium or potassium stearate) | O/W |
| | Divalent soaps (calcium oleate) | W/O |
| **Cationic** | Cetrimide, benzalkonium chloride | O/W (mainly in external preparations) |
| **Non-ionic** | Polysorbates (Tweens) | O/W |
| | Sorbitan esters (Spans) | W/O |
| **Finely divided solids** | Bentonite, magnesium hydroxide, aluminium hydroxide (wetted mainly by water) | O/W |
| | Carbon black, talc (wetted by oil) | W/O |

**Bancroft's rule:** the phase in which the emulsifier is more soluble becomes the continuous phase.

### HLB system

The **hydrophile–lipophile balance** (HLB) number (0–20) shows the balance between water-loving and oil-loving parts of a surfactant.

| HLB range | Use |
| --- | --- |
| 1–3 | Antifoaming agents |
| 3–6 | W/O emulsifiers |
| 7–9 | Wetting agents |
| 8–18 | O/W emulsifiers |
| 13–16 | Detergents |
| 15–18 | Solubilisers |

**Blending example.** An oil needs a required HLB of 12. Use Span 80 (HLB 4.3) and Tween 80 (HLB 15.0). Let x = fraction of Tween 80.
15.0x + 4.3(1 − x) = 12 → 10.7x = 7.7 → x = 0.72.
So use **72% Tween 80 and 28% Span 80** (for 5 g of emulsifier: 3.6 g Tween 80 + 1.4 g Span 80).

### Tests to identify the type of emulsion

| Test | Procedure | O/W result | W/O result |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Dilution test** | Add the emulsion to water | Mixes easily (water is continuous) | Does not mix; stays as lumps |
| **Dye solubility test** | Add a water-soluble dye (amaranth or methylene blue) and look under the microscope | Continuous phase coloured, globules colourless | Globules coloured, background colourless |
| | Add an oil-soluble dye (Sudan III) | Globules red | Continuous phase red |
| **Conductivity test** | Dip two electrodes with a bulb in circuit | Bulb glows (water conducts) | Bulb does not glow |
| **Fluorescence test** | View under UV light (many oils fluoresce) | Only dots fluoresce | Whole field fluoresces |
| **Cobalt chloride paper** | Dip filter paper soaked in CoCl2 and dried (blue) | Turns pink (water continuous) | Stays blue |

### Methods of preparation

| Method | How | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Dry gum (continental) method** | Triturate oil with dry gum (acacia), then add all the water at once and triturate rapidly until a clicking primary emulsion forms; dilute | Ratio oil : water : gum = **4 : 2 : 1** for fixed oils, **3 : 2 : 1** for mineral oil, **2 : 2 : 1** for volatile oils |
| **Wet gum (English) method** | Make a mucilage of gum with water, then add oil in small portions with trituration | Same ratios; slower but suits larger batches |
| **Bottle (Forbes bottle) method** | Shake oil and powdered acacia in a dry bottle, add water, shake vigorously | For **volatile oils** and low-viscosity oils |
| **Nascent soap (in situ soap) method** | A fatty acid in the oil reacts with an alkali (for example oleic acid in a vegetable oil with lime water) to form soap at the interface | Calcium soaps give W/O (oily calamine lotion, lime liniment) |
| **Mechanical methods** | Mixers, homogenisers, colloid mills, ultrasonifiers | Industrial scale, fine and uniform globules |

The **primary emulsion** is the thick, white, clicking emulsion formed first; it is then diluted with the rest of the water.

### Stability problems and how to overcome them

| Problem | What happens | Reversible? | Remedy |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Creaming** (upward) or **sedimentation** (downward) | Globules collect at the top or bottom without joining; obeys Stokes' law | Yes, by shaking | Reduce globule size (homogenise), increase viscosity of continuous phase, reduce density difference |
| **Flocculation** | Globules cluster loosely | Yes | Adequate emulsifier film, suitable charge |
| **Cracking (coalescence / breaking)** | Globules merge and the phases separate permanently | No | Enough emulsifier, avoid incompatible additives (electrolytes, alcohol, opposite-charge surfactants), avoid heat, freezing and microbial growth |
| **Phase inversion** | O/W changes to W/O or the reverse | Sometimes | Keep the phase volume ratio suitable (internal phase usually below about 60–70%), avoid adding substances that change the emulsifier (for example calcium salts with sodium soaps) |
| **Microbial contamination** | Water phase and natural gums support growth | No | Preservatives effective in the water phase (parabens), clean manufacture |
| **Oxidation (rancidity)** | Oils turn rancid | No | Antioxidants (BHA, BHT, tocopherol), air-tight full containers |

## Remember

- Simple Syrup IP = 66.7% w/w sucrose, self-preserving. Elixir = clear, sweet, hydroalcoholic. Throat paints use glycerin. Nasal drops: aqueous, isotonic, never oily.
- Liniment = with friction, never on broken skin; lotion = without friction.
- Stokes' law: v = d²(ρs − ρo)g/18η — smaller particles, higher viscosity, smaller density difference slow settling.
- Flocculated: fast settling, loose easily redispersed sediment; deflocculated: slow settling but hard cake. Controlled flocculation is the aim. F = Vu/Vo, β = F/F∞.
- Emulsion tests: dilution, dye, conductivity, fluorescence, cobalt chloride paper.
- Dry gum ratios 4:2:1 (fixed oil), 3:2:1 (mineral oil), 2:2:1 (volatile oil).
- Creaming is reversible; cracking is not. HLB 3–6 W/O, 8–18 O/W.

# Unit 4: Suppositories and pharmaceutical incompatibilities

The first half of this unit deals with suppositories: their types, bases, methods of making them and the displacement value numerical, which is asked almost every year. The second half covers incompatibilities, the undesirable changes that happen when ingredients of a prescription react with each other or with the body.

## 4.1 Suppositories

**Suppository:** a solid unit dosage form of suitable shape and size for insertion into a body cavity (rectum, vagina or urethra), where it **melts, softens or dissolves** to release the drug for local or systemic action.

### Types

| Type | Site | Usual weight / shape | Example use |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Rectal suppositories** | Rectum | About 1 g for children and 2 g for adults; torpedo or bullet shaped (tapered at one or both ends) | Glycerol (laxative), paracetamol, diclofenac, antiemetics, haemorrhoid preparations |
| **Vaginal suppositories (pessaries)** | Vagina | Larger, 3–8 g; oval, conical or globular | Antifungals (clotrimazole), antiseptics, contraceptives |
| **Urethral suppositories (bougies)** | Urethra | Thin pencil shape | Antiseptics, local anaesthetics (rare now) |
| **Nasal / ear cones** | Nose, ear | Small cones | Rarely used |

### Advantages

1. Useful when the **oral route is not possible**: vomiting, unconsciousness, young children, before and after surgery, difficulty in swallowing.
2. Drugs that **irritate the stomach** or are **destroyed by stomach acid or enzymes** can be given.
3. Drug absorbed from the lower rectum partly **avoids first-pass metabolism** in the liver (veins of the lower rectum drain into the general circulation).
4. **Local action** in haemorrhoids, constipation and vaginal infections.
5. Bitter taste and smell are avoided.

### Disadvantages

1. Not acceptable to many patients; embarrassing to use.
2. Absorption can be slow, irregular and incomplete; affected by faeces in the rectum.
3. Can cause local irritation (proctitis).
4. Bases may melt in hot weather; need cool storage.
5. Making them is more difficult and costly than tablets.

### Ideal properties of a suppository base

- Melts at **body temperature** (just below 37 °C) or dissolves in body fluids.
- Non-toxic, non-irritant to mucous membranes.
- Compatible with a wide range of drugs; releases the drug readily.
- Stable on storage: does not turn rancid or change shape; keeps firm at room temperature.
- **Contracts on cooling** so the suppository leaves the mould easily.
- Has a narrow gap between melting and solidifying points; can be moulded by hand, by pouring or by compression.

### Types of suppository bases

**A. Fatty (oleaginous) bases** — melt at body temperature.

| Base | Notes |
| --- | --- |
| **Theobroma oil (cocoa butter)** | Fat from roasted cocoa seeds; melts at about 30–35 °C. Pleasant, bland, non-irritant. **Polymorphic**: if heated much above 36 °C and cooled fast, it forms unstable crystal forms of low melting point, so the suppositories do not set or melt too easily. Melt it on a water bath at low temperature (creamy melt) to keep the stable form. Other drawbacks: becomes rancid, does not contract much on cooling (mould must be lubricated), softens in hot climates, melting point lowered by some drugs (chloral hydrate) |
| **Synthetic and semi-synthetic fats** | Hydrogenated vegetable oils and fractionated fats (hard fat bases sold under trade names). Fewer polymorphism problems, do not turn rancid easily, contract well, need no lubricant |
| **Emulsified bases** | Fats with emulsifiers, which help take up water |

**B. Water-soluble and water-miscible bases** — dissolve or disperse in body fluids.

| Base | Notes |
| --- | --- |
| **Glycero-gelatin base** | Gelatin, glycerin and water (glycerol suppositories contain about 14% gelatin and 70% glycerol). Dissolves slowly in rectal fluid; good for vaginal pessaries. Drawbacks: hygroscopic (draws water from mucosa, causing irritation), supports microbial growth (needs preservative), takes longer to make, must be stored in airtight containers |
| **Polyethylene glycols (PEG, macrogols)** | Blends of high and low molecular weight PEGs give the required hardness. Dissolve in body fluids; stable; no refrigeration needed; do not support microbes. Drawbacks: can irritate the mucosa (moisten the suppository before insertion), incompatible with some drugs (for example phenols, benzocaine, some antibiotics) |
| **Soap glycerin** | Glycerin hardened with sodium stearate; used for laxative suppositories |

**C. Other bases:** surfactant bases (polyoxyethylene derivatives), which spread and disperse.

### Methods of preparation

**1. Hand rolling (manual moulding)** — the oldest method. The drug is mixed with grated base in a mortar into a plastic mass, rolled into a cylinder on a tile and cut and shaped by hand. Only for small numbers; mainly with theobroma oil.

**2. Compression moulding** — grated base and drug are mixed and pressed into a mould in a cylinder by a screw or wheel. No heat, so suitable for **heat-labile drugs** and insoluble substances. Cold compression avoids sedimentation of drug.

**3. Fusion (pour moulding)** — the most common method, used for all base types.

1. **Calibrate the mould** with the chosen base (fill with plain base, weigh the suppositories).
2. **Lubricate** the mould if needed: for theobroma oil use soap spirit or a soap–glycerin–alcohol solution; for glycero-gelatin use liquid paraffin or an oil. Synthetic fats need no lubricant.
3. **Melt the base** on a water bath at the lowest temperature possible.
4. **Incorporate the drug**: dissolve soluble drugs in the melted base; finely powder insoluble drugs and levigate with a little melted base; calculate the base needed using the **displacement value**.
5. **Pour** into the mould when the mixture is near its setting point (creamy), with slight overfilling to allow for contraction.
6. **Cool** (in a refrigerator if needed), trim the excess with a warm spatula, open the mould and remove the suppositories.
7. Pack individually in foil or plastic, label and store in a cool place.

```text
   SUPPOSITORY MOULD (split, 6 cavities)
    ___________________________
   |  ( )  ( )  ( )  ( )  ( )  ( ) |  <- torpedo-shaped cavities
   |___________________________|
      two halves held by a screw;
      overfill, cool, trim the top, open
```

### Calibration of the mould

The nominal size of a mould (for example "1 g") refers to theobroma oil. Each mould must be calibrated with the actual base: prepare a set of plain suppositories, weigh them and find the average weight. A glycero-gelatin base is denser, so the same mould holds roughly 1.2 times the weight of theobroma oil.

## 4.2 Displacement value

When a drug is added, it **takes up space** in the mould and pushes out (displaces) some base. Because the drug and base have different densities, the weight of base displaced is not equal to the weight of drug.

**Displacement value (DV):** the number of parts by weight of a drug that displaces **one part by weight of the base** (usually theobroma oil).

DV = weight of drug ÷ weight of base displaced by it

A drug with DV 5 (for example zinc oxide is often quoted as 5) is dense: 5 g of it occupies the space of only 1 g of base.

### Calculating the amount of base needed

**Base needed = (number of suppositories × mould capacity) − (total weight of drug ÷ DV)**

**Example 1.** Prepare 10 suppositories each containing 300 mg zinc oxide in a 1 g mould (DV of zinc oxide = 5, given).
Total drug = 10 × 0.3 = 3.0 g. Base displaced = 3.0 ÷ 5 = 0.6 g.
Base needed = 10 × 1 − 0.6 = **9.4 g theobroma oil**.
In practice prepare for 2 extra (12 suppositories): drug 3.6 g; base = 12 − 3.6 ÷ 5 = 12 − 0.72 = **11.28 g**.

**Example 2.** Six suppositories each containing 200 mg of a drug, DV = 2, 1 g mould.
Drug = 6 × 0.2 = 1.2 g. Base displaced = 1.2 ÷ 2 = 0.6 g. Base = 6 − 0.6 = **5.4 g**.

**Example 3 (two drugs).** Ten suppositories (1 g mould), each with 100 mg of drug A (DV 1.5) and 250 mg of drug B (DV 2.5).
A = 1.0 g → displaces 1.0 ÷ 1.5 = 0.667 g. B = 2.5 g → displaces 2.5 ÷ 2.5 = 1.0 g.
Base = 10 − (0.667 + 1.0) = **8.33 g**.

### Determination of displacement value

1. Prepare 6 plain (unmedicated) suppositories and weigh them: weight = **a** g.
2. Prepare 6 suppositories containing a known percentage (x%) of drug in the same mould and weigh them: weight = **b** g.
3. Drug in medicated suppositories = b × x ÷ 100 = **c** g.
4. Base in medicated suppositories = b − c.
5. Base displaced by drug = a − (b − c).
6. **DV = c ÷ [a − (b − c)]**.

**Worked example.** 6 plain suppositories weigh 6.0 g. 6 suppositories with 40% drug weigh 8.5 g.
Drug = 8.5 × 40 ÷ 100 = 3.4 g. Base = 8.5 − 3.4 = 5.1 g. Base displaced = 6.0 − 5.1 = 0.9 g.
DV = 3.4 ÷ 0.9 = **3.78**.

## 4.3 Evaluation of suppositories

| Test | What it checks |
| --- | --- |
| **Visual examination** | Uniform colour and shape, no cracks, fissures, pits, fat bloom or sedimentation of drug (cut lengthwise to see drug distribution) |
| **Uniformity of weight** | Weigh 20 suppositories individually; compare with the average weight within pharmacopoeial limits |
| **Content uniformity / assay** | Drug content of individual suppositories |
| **Melting range / macro melting range test** | Temperature at which the suppository melts (for fatty bases) |
| **Liquefaction (softening) time test** | Time taken to soften and lose shape at 37 °C under a weight (for example U-tube or rectal-simulation apparatus) |
| **Breaking (hardness / mechanical strength) test** | Weight needed to break the suppository; checks it will withstand handling |
| **Disintegration test** | Time to melt, soften or dissolve at 37 °C in water (pharmacopoeial apparatus); fatty-base suppositories should disintegrate within about 30 minutes and water-soluble ones within about 60 minutes |
| **Dissolution / drug release** | Release of drug into a medium, often using a basket or membrane |
| **Stability** | Changes on storage: hardness, melting point, appearance |

## 4.4 Pharmaceutical incompatibilities

**Incompatibility:** an undesirable change that takes place when two or more substances are mixed, or when a drug is given with another drug, so that the product becomes unacceptable in **appearance, stability, safety or therapeutic effect**.

Incompatibilities may be **intentional** (the prescriber means the reaction to happen, for example effervescence in effervescent preparations or forming a soap in situ) or **unintentional** (an error that the pharmacist must spot and correct).

### Classification

```text
                      INCOMPATIBILITIES
         ____________________|____________________
        |                    |                    |
    Physical             Chemical            Therapeutic
   (visible change,     (chemical reaction   (undesired effect
    no new compound)     new substance)       in the body)
```

### A. Physical incompatibility

A visible physical change without a new chemical substance. Usually corrected by a change in the order of mixing, a solvent, an emulsifier or a suspending agent.

| Type | Example | Correction |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Insolubility** | Resinous tinctures (for example compound benzoin tincture) precipitate resin when added to water | Add slowly with a suspending agent (tragacanth) |
| **Immiscibility** | Oils with water | Emulsify with a suitable emulsifying agent |
| **Liquefaction (eutectic)** | Camphor, menthol, phenol, thymol together in powders | Dispense separately or use an absorbent (light MgO, kaolin) |
| **Precipitation by change of solvent** | Alcoholic solution diluted with water | Use a cosolvent, add slowly with stirring |
| **Salting out** | High salt concentration throws a dissolved substance out of solution | Dilute or reduce salt |
| **Adsorption** | Drugs adsorbed on kaolin, charcoal or containers | Change the formulation or separate dosing |
| **Hygroscopic or efflorescent changes** | Powders become damp | Use dried forms, airtight packing |

### B. Chemical incompatibility

A chemical reaction forms a new substance. It may be visible (precipitate, colour, gas, heat) or invisible (loss of potency).

| Type | Example |
| --- | --- |
| **Precipitation** | Alkaloidal salts (for example quinine) with alkalis precipitate the free base; tannic acid precipitates alkaloids and proteins; sodium salts of barbiturates (sodium phenobarbitone) precipitate the free acid in acid solution |
| **Effervescence / gas evolution** | Sodium bicarbonate with acids or acid salts gives CO2 (bottle may burst); carbonates with acids |
| **Oxidation–reduction** | Adrenaline, phenols and ascorbic acid oxidise and change colour in light or alkali |
| **Hydrolysis** | Aspirin and esters such as procaine break down in moist or alkaline conditions |
| **Colour change** | Iron salts give dark colours with tannins and salicylates |
| **Explosive or fire-risk combinations** | Strong oxidising agents (potassium permanganate, potassium chlorate) with reducing agents or organic matter such as glycerin, sugar, sulphur, tannic acid |
| **Complexation / chelation** | Tetracyclines bind calcium, magnesium, aluminium and iron ions |
| **Cementation** | Some insoluble powders set into a hard mass in liquids |

**Ways of handling chemical incompatibility:** change the order of mixing, dilute the reacting ingredients, add a suspending agent to make an unavoidable precipitate diffusible, adjust pH, use an alternative salt or drug (with the prescriber's consent), dispense separately, protect from light and air, or for effervescent mixtures let the gas escape before closing the bottle.

### C. Therapeutic incompatibility

The combination gives an effect in the patient different from the one intended.

| Type | Example |
| --- | --- |
| **Antagonism** | A beta-blocker with a beta-agonist bronchodilator; a cholinergic drug with an anticholinergic drug |
| **Synergism leading to toxicity** | Two central nervous system depressants (sedative with alcohol); two drugs that lower potassium |
| **Interference with absorption** | Tetracycline with antacids, milk or iron salts (chelation) |
| **Contraindication** | Aspirin in a patient with a peptic ulcer; certain drugs in pregnancy |
| **Overdose or wrong dose** | Dose above the maximum, wrong frequency |
| **Wrong drug or wrong combination** | Sound-alike names, duplicate drugs of the same class |

The pharmacist must contact the prescriber about any therapeutic incompatibility. It must never be "corrected" without the prescriber's agreement.

## Remember

- Rectal suppositories about 1 g (child) and 2 g (adult); pessaries 3–8 g.
- Theobroma oil melts at about 30–35 °C and is polymorphic: melt gently (creamy melt). Glycero-gelatin is hygroscopic and needs a preservative; PEG bases dissolve rather than melt.
- Methods: hand rolling, compression moulding (heat-sensitive drugs), fusion / pour moulding (most common). Calibrate and lubricate the mould.
- DV = drug ÷ base displaced. Base needed = N × mould capacity − (total drug ÷ DV). DV from data = c ÷ [a − (b − c)].
- Evaluation: appearance, weight uniformity, content, melting range, liquefaction time, breaking test, disintegration, dissolution.
- Incompatibility: physical (no new substance), chemical (new substance), therapeutic (unwanted effect in the body); never change a therapeutic incompatibility without the prescriber.

# Unit 5: Semisolid dosage forms

Semisolids are applied to the skin or mucous membranes for protection, moisturising and treatment of skin disease, and sometimes for drug action deeper in the tissues. This unit covers the types of semisolids, how drugs pass through the skin, ointment bases, methods of preparing ointments, pastes, creams and gels, the excipients used and how the products are evaluated. Classification of ointment bases and factors affecting skin penetration are the most frequently asked topics.

## 5.1 Definitions and classification

**Semisolid dosage forms:** preparations of soft consistency, intended for application to the skin or certain mucous membranes (eye, nose, rectum, vagina), that keep their shape at rest but spread easily under pressure.

| Dosage form | Definition | Examples |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Ointment** | Soft, greasy (or water-soluble) semisolid with drug dissolved or dispersed in a single-phase base | Sulphur ointment, simple ointment, Whitfield's ointment |
| **Cream** | Semisolid **emulsion** (O/W or W/O), less greasy and more cosmetically acceptable | Cold cream (W/O), vanishing cream (O/W), cetrimide cream |
| **Paste** | Ointment with a **high proportion of finely powdered solids** (often 20–50% or more), stiff and less greasy | Zinc oxide paste, compound zinc paste, Lassar's paste |
| **Gel (jelly)** | Semisolid made of a liquid held in a three-dimensional network of a gelling agent; usually transparent | Carbopol gel, diclofenac gel, lignocaine gel, sodium alginate gel |
| **Poultice (cataplasm)** | Soft paste applied hot to reduce inflammation | Kaolin poultice |
| **Plasters** | Adhesive material spread on a backing | Medicated plasters |

**Classification by site of use:** dermatological (skin), ophthalmic (eye ointments, sterile), nasal, rectal, vaginal.

**Classification by depth of action:**

- **Epidermic (surface) action:** protective, emollient, antiseptic (zinc oxide, calamine).
- **Endodermic action:** drug penetrates the skin layers (corticosteroids, antifungals, local anaesthetics).
- **Diadermic action:** drug passes through the skin into the blood for systemic action (nitroglycerin ointment).

## 5.2 Structure of skin and dermal penetration of drugs

```text
   SKIN (cross-section)
   ---------------------------------------------- surface
   | Stratum corneum  (10-20 µm, dead keratinised  |  <- main barrier
   |                   cells + lipid "mortar")     |
   | Viable epidermis (living cells, no blood)     |
   |-----------------------------------------------|
   | Dermis (blood vessels, nerves, hair follicles,|
   |         sweat glands, sebaceous glands)       |
   |-----------------------------------------------|
   | Subcutaneous fat (hypodermis)                 |
   ----------------------------------------------
```

The **stratum corneum** is the main barrier. It is often described as "bricks and mortar": dead keratin-filled cells (bricks) in a matrix of lipids (mortar).

### Mechanisms (routes) of penetration

1. **Transepidermal route** (main route)
   - **Intercellular**: drug diffuses through the lipid channels between the cells — the main path for most drugs.
   - **Transcellular (intracellular)**: drug passes through the cells and the lipids in turn; favours hydrophilic drugs to a small extent.
2. **Transappendageal (shunt) route** — through **hair follicles and sebaceous glands** (transfollicular) and **sweat ducts**. These make up only a small fraction of the skin surface, but they matter early after application and for large or ionised molecules.

Passive diffusion follows **Fick's law**:

**J = D × K × ΔC ÷ h**

J = flux (amount crossing per unit area per unit time), D = diffusion coefficient in the membrane, K = partition coefficient between membrane and vehicle, ΔC = concentration difference across the membrane, h = thickness of the membrane.

### Factors influencing dermal penetration

**A. Drug (physicochemical) factors**

| Factor | Effect |
| --- | --- |
| Molecular size | Small molecules (molecular weight below about 500) penetrate better |
| Partition coefficient | A balance of oil and water solubility is best; moderately lipophilic drugs (log P about 1–3) cross the skin well |
| Solubility and concentration | Higher concentration in the vehicle (up to saturation) gives a higher driving force |
| Ionisation (pKa) | Un-ionised molecules cross more easily |
| Melting point | Low-melting drugs are more soluble in the skin lipids |

**B. Vehicle (base) factors**

| Factor | Effect |
| --- | --- |
| Release of drug from base | The drug must leave the base; if it is very soluble in the base, it stays there |
| **Occlusion** | Greasy bases and occlusive dressings stop water loss, so the stratum corneum hydrates and swells, increasing penetration |
| Penetration enhancers | Propylene glycol, alcohols, DMSO, oleic acid, urea, surfactants loosen the lipid barrier |
| pH of the vehicle | Controls ionisation of the drug |

**C. Skin (biological) factors**

| Factor | Effect |
| --- | --- |
| **Hydration** | Hydrated skin is more permeable |
| Site of application | Thin skin (scrotum, face, eyelids) is more permeable than thick skin (palms, soles) |
| Condition of skin | Damaged, diseased or burnt skin allows much more absorption |
| Age | Infants (larger surface area per kg) and the elderly absorb differently; infants are at risk of toxicity |
| Blood flow | Higher blood flow removes drug faster and keeps the gradient |
| Temperature | Warm skin is more permeable |
| Skin metabolism | Enzymes in skin may break down some drugs |

**D. Method of application:** amount applied, area, rubbing and time of contact.

## 5.3 Ointment bases

The base is the vehicle in which the drug is incorporated. It controls release, occlusion, ease of application and stability.

### Ideal properties of an ointment base

- Non-irritant, non-sensitising, inert and compatible with drugs.
- Stable; does not turn rancid.
- Releases the drug easily.
- Easy to apply and remove; does not stain.
- Smooth, of suitable consistency, not affected much by temperature.
- Free from microbial contamination.

### Classification of ointment bases

| Class | Properties | Examples |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **1. Oleaginous (hydrocarbon) bases** | Greasy, anhydrous, occlusive, emollient, do not absorb water, hard to wash off, do not dry out, cheap and stable | White and yellow soft paraffin (petrolatum), hard paraffin, liquid paraffin, vegetable oils, animal fats, beeswax |
| **2. Absorption bases** | Can absorb water to form W/O emulsions. (a) **Anhydrous** types that take up water; (b) **W/O emulsion** types that already contain water but can take more. Greasy, not easily washed | (a) Wool fat (anhydrous lanolin), wool alcohols ointment, hydrophilic petrolatum; (b) hydrous wool fat, cold cream |
| **3. Water-removable (emulsion O/W) bases** | O/W emulsions; washable with water, non-greasy, can be diluted with water, absorb exudates. Less occlusive | Hydrophilic ointment, emulsifying ointment (when made into a cream), vanishing cream |
| **4. Water-soluble bases** | Contain no fat; completely water-soluble and washable; non-occlusive; do not stain | Polyethylene glycol (macrogol) ointment |

```text
   Increasing water-washability ------------------------>
   Hydrocarbon  -->  Absorption  -->  O/W removable  -->  Water-soluble
   Increasing occlusion and greasiness <------------------
```

### Choice of base

Depends on: desired action (surface protection needs an occlusive base; deep penetration needs a base that releases the drug and hydrates skin), nature of the skin condition (dry scaly lesions → greasy base; wet oozing lesions → washable or drying base or paste), stability and compatibility of the drug, ease of application and patient acceptance.

## 5.4 Preparation of ointments

| Method | Used when | Procedure |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Trituration (incorporation)** | Base is soft and drug is a solid or small liquid quantity | Finely powder the drug, levigate it with a little base (or liquid paraffin) on a tile with a spatula until smooth, then add the rest of the base in portions (geometric dilution). Soluble drugs may be dissolved in a little water or solvent first |
| **Fusion** | Base contains hard ingredients (waxes, hard paraffin, wool fat) or the drug is soluble in the melted base | Melt the ingredients in order of decreasing melting point (highest first) on a water bath, add soluble drugs, stir continuously while cooling until it sets (to avoid lumps and graininess). Do not over-heat |
| **Chemical reaction** | A reaction forms the active ingredient | Example: iodine ointments in which iodine reacts with an oil or fatty acid, giving a non-staining product |
| **Emulsification** | Creams and emulsion ointments | Heat oil phase and aqueous phase separately to about the same temperature (about 70–75 °C), add one to the other with stirring, stir until cool |

**Example formula: simple ointment** (an oleaginous base used in fusion practice) contains wool fat, hard paraffin and cetostearyl alcohol in white or yellow soft paraffin.

**Example: Sulphur ointment** — precipitated sulphur (10%) incorporated in simple ointment by trituration; used for scabies and fungal skin infections.

## 5.5 Preparation of pastes

- Pastes are stiff because of a high solid content. They stay in place, absorb exudates and protect the skin. They are less occlusive than ointments because the powder forms channels.
- **Bases:** hydrocarbon (soft paraffin) for fatty pastes; glycerin or a gel for non-greasy pastes.
- **Method:** finely sift the powders, triturate them with a portion of the base (often warmed) or with liquid paraffin to a smooth paste, add the remaining base, or use fusion when the base needs melting.
- Examples: **Compound zinc paste** (zinc oxide and starch in white soft paraffin), **Zinc and salicylic acid paste (Lassar's paste)** (zinc oxide, starch and 2% salicylic acid in white soft paraffin), **Coal tar paste**.

## 5.6 Preparation of creams

- Creams are emulsions: **O/W (vanishing)** creams are non-greasy and washable; **W/O (cold)** creams are emollient and cooling as the water evaporates.
- **Method:** prepare oil phase (oils, waxes, oil-soluble emulsifier and drug) and aqueous phase (water, water-soluble emulsifier, humectant, preservative) separately; heat both to about 70–75 °C; add the internal phase to the external phase with stirring; stir until cool; add volatile ingredients and perfume below about 40 °C; homogenise if needed.
- **Cold cream:** beeswax and liquid paraffin with borax and water; borax reacts with free fatty acids in beeswax to form sodium soap at the interface.
- **Vanishing cream:** stearic acid partly neutralised with an alkali (potassium hydroxide or triethanolamine) to form soap; leaves a thin non-greasy film.

## 5.7 Preparation of gels

- **Gels** contain a gelling agent that forms a network trapping the liquid.
- **Gelling agents:** natural (tragacanth, sodium alginate, pectin, gelatin, xanthan), semi-synthetic cellulose derivatives (methylcellulose, HPMC, sodium CMC), synthetic polymers (**carbomers / carbopol**, poloxamers), inorganic (bentonite, colloidal silica).
- **Carbopol gel method:** sprinkle the carbomer powder slowly on water with constant stirring (avoid lumps), allow it to swell, then **neutralise with triethanolamine or sodium hydroxide** to a pH of about 6–7. The acidic polymer chains ionise, uncoil by charge repulsion and the dispersion thickens suddenly into a clear gel.
- **Single-phase gels** (polymer uniformly spread, clear) and **two-phase gels** (small discrete particles such as aluminium hydroxide gel).
- Problems: **syneresis** (gel contracts and squeezes out liquid), swelling, microbial growth (add preservative).

## 5.8 Excipients used in semisolid dosage forms

| Excipient | Function | Examples |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Bases | Vehicle | Soft paraffin, wool fat, PEGs, emulsifying wax |
| Emulsifying agents | Form creams | Emulsifying wax, cetostearyl alcohol with sodium lauryl sulphate, polysorbates, sorbitan esters, wool alcohols |
| Stiffening agents | Increase consistency | Hard paraffin, beeswax, cetyl and stearyl alcohol |
| Gelling agents | Form gels | Carbomer, HPMC, sodium CMC, tragacanth |
| Neutralising agents | Thicken carbomer gels | Triethanolamine, sodium hydroxide |
| Humectants | Prevent drying, keep skin moist | Glycerin, propylene glycol, sorbitol |
| Preservatives | Prevent microbial growth (water-containing products) | Methyl and propyl parabens, chlorocresol, benzalkonium chloride, phenoxyethanol |
| Antioxidants | Prevent rancidity of fats and oils | BHA, BHT, tocopherol, propyl gallate |
| Penetration enhancers | Increase drug passage through skin | Propylene glycol, DMSO, oleic acid, urea, ethanol, isopropyl myristate |
| Buffers | Maintain pH | Citrate and phosphate buffers |
| Chelating agents | Bind metal ions | Disodium edetate |
| Perfumes and colours | Acceptability | Rose oil, lavender oil |

## 5.9 Evaluation of semisolid dosage forms

| Test | Purpose and method |
| --- | --- |
| **Appearance and homogeneity** | Colour, odour, texture; smear on a glass plate to check for grittiness or lumps |
| **Drug content uniformity** | Assay samples from different parts of the container |
| **pH** | pH meter on a dispersion; skin-compatible pH |
| **Viscosity / rheology** | Brookfield (rotational) viscometer; semisolids show non-Newtonian (plastic or pseudoplastic, thixotropic) flow |
| **Consistency (penetration test)** | **Cone penetrometer**: depth a standard cone sinks into the sample in a fixed time |
| **Spreadability** | Parallel-plate method: time for a top slide to move a fixed distance under a weight. **S = M × L ÷ T** (M = weight tied to the upper slide, L = length moved, T = time); shorter time means better spreading |
| **Extrudability** | Weight or pressure needed to squeeze a ribbon of product from a collapsible tube |
| **Drug release (in vitro diffusion)** | **Franz diffusion cell**: product placed on a membrane (synthetic or skin) over a receptor fluid at 32–37 °C; samples analysed over time |
| **Skin irritation / sensitisation** | Patch tests on animals or volunteers |
| **Microbial limit test / sterility** | Absence of specified organisms; ophthalmic ointments must be sterile and checked for metal particles |
| **Minimum fill** | Contents of the container not below the labelled amount |
| **Stability** | Phase separation, colour, odour, pH, viscosity, drug content at accelerated and normal storage; freeze–thaw cycling for creams |
| **Occlusivity / water absorption** | Ability to prevent water loss; water number of a base (amount of water a base can hold) |

**Spreadability example.** A 50 g weight pulls the upper slide 7.5 cm in 10 s.
S = 50 × 7.5 ÷ 10 = **37.5 g·cm/s**.

## Remember

- Ointment = single-phase greasy base; cream = emulsion; paste = high solid content; gel = liquid in a polymer network.
- Stratum corneum is the main barrier; main route is intercellular (transepidermal); appendages give a minor shunt route. Fick's law J = DKΔC/h.
- Penetration rises with small size, balanced log P, high concentration, occlusion, hydration, damaged or thin skin.
- Ointment bases: hydrocarbon, absorption (anhydrous or W/O), water-removable (O/W), water-soluble (PEG).
- Methods: trituration, fusion (melt highest melting point first), chemical reaction, emulsification (both phases at 70–75 °C).
- Carbopol gels form when the polymer is neutralised (triethanolamine) to about pH 6–7.
- Evaluation: content, pH, viscosity, penetrometer, spreadability S = ML/T, extrudability, Franz cell release, irritation, microbial limits.
